utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Ms. Kravetz, you promised us some entertainment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm not sure how entertaining I will be but I'll try my best. Your Honours, I just wanted to raise a matter of concern regarding the next witness. One of the issues or topics that is listed in the 65 ter summary for the next witness is that he will speak about a meeting in March 1999 between General Ojdanic and General Drewienkiewicz, also known as General DZ. As Your Honours remember, General DZ testified before this Court in June of last year, and during his testimony in this trial the Defence did not put any questions to him about this specific issue. Now, it is our view - and this is the concern we have - that if the evidence of the following witness is brought to contradict the testimony of General DZ, the proper and fair way to have proceeded during his testimony for the Defence to have put questions to him on this matter in order to allow him to comment and provide his version of events. And we believe that that would have been the fair way to proceed because that would have assisted Your Honours in assessing the credibility of contradictory evidence that is brought in regards -- with regards to his testimony. That did not happen during his testimony, and so we just wanted to raise this matter and leave it for Your Honours to deal with in the best way you consider necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have reason to anticipate that the evidence of the witness will differ from that of the previous witness in some material way? We don't have any indication of the nature of the evidence of this witness except on extremely brief and broad outline.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That is true, and that's why I'm raising it at this stage is to alert Your Honours. We don't have more details about what he would say about this meeting, but I -- we did not lead any evidence on this specific meeting, and that is why we believe, if this was an issue that the Defence intended to broach, they should have raised it during the testimony of General DZ. This is not a matter that was addressed specifically. And had it been raised during his testimony, it is our view that General DZ may have provided a different version of accounts than the one this witness will provide. But I do agree with Your Honours that the summary is very brief, and it may be that this witness's evidence will not be contradicting that of General DZ. Just based on the summary alone, I'm not able to tell that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you're speaking essentially out of caution at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I am, Your Honours, that's why I'm raising it as a matter of concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I believe there is no cause for concern. It was an omission, that is to say, the statement -- this is a meeting between General Ojdanic and General DZ in March 1999. This witness attended the meeting. I think it was in November or December 1998. We have the actual date. But I can tell you in advance that this is some seminar that was organised in March 1999 where Mr. Drewienkiewicz lectured. So the witness is mentioning it in that context only. Ojdanic was not present at all at the seminar, so I believe there will be no problems whatsoever in this regard. As for what was said whether we had any questions for General Drewienkiewicz at the time, believe me, the Defence did not even know about that seminar in March 1999. And I believe that it doesn't really matter. Drewienkiewicz was just present, and this is a mistake. This is simply an error, the fact that it was called a meeting. It was a seminar. So you will hear the witness and, if necessary, I'll even cut that part short. But anyway, I think there's really no need for concern or is there any need for General DZ to testify again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, with that re-assurance, we'll proceed. And we expect that the evidence of the witness will be no more than you have indicated about that occasion, whether it be a seminar or a meeting. Ms. Kravetz, you're ready to proceed? That could be useful, couldn't it? It could be useful. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't mind. I certainly don't mind. Yes, Ms. Kravetz can proceed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have a very generous spirit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Are the microphones on for the witness? Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Novakovic, could you please give us your personal details for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Kosta Novakovic. I was born on the 6th of December, 1949, in Bijeljina, the municipality of Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we start working, would you like me to call you colonel or Mr. Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Novakovic, you and I speak the same language. The purpose of these proceedings is to have your testimony properly recorded in the transcript as interpreted. So I will try to speak at a pace that is proper for having this job done as it should be, and I'm kindly asking you to do the same. The easiest way of doing it is to wait for me to finish my question and to finish -- and to see that the transcript has finished recording my question, and then you start answering. Mr. Novakovic, can you tell us what your profession is today?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a retiree. I used to be a military officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In which army did you serve at your point of retirement?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I retired from the Army of Yugoslavia and I held the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your education, Mr. Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: First I completed elementary school, then high school, then the military academy, the higher military political school, post-graduate studies. My master's degree was entitled the international legal status of national minorities. And my doctorate was entitled national minorities and defence in Yugoslavia, in the context of national minorities, defence, and security of multi-ethnic countries, that is to say that I hold a doctorate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us which positions you held in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and in 1999, I was an independent desk officer in the first administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, that's the operations administration. To be more specific, I headed the desk for combat-readiness for the 2nd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to the position that you referred to just now, during 1998 and 1999 did you have any other special duties?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Towards the end of 1998, specifically in the month of October, on the basis of a special order of the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, I was appointed as member of a team for relations between the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia with the missions of the OSCE and NATO for verification in Kosovo and Metohija. I was involved in that team from October 1998 until March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have document D006-1479, and I would like to ask the Honourable Trial Chamber to allow the witness to use the hard copy that has been prepared for him so that we could proceed more efficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, this document is number 1 in your binder. It is a document on the appointment of the VJ team for liaison with the OSCE and NATO missions from the 22nd of October, 1998. It was an order by General Momcilo Perisic. Mr. Novakovic, can you tell us in relation to this document what kind of a team composition is this, what were the tasks before this team?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: This was an expert team. We can say it was an expert group or a commission, that is to say that it consisted primarily of experts from different fields, whose task was to prepare proposals, orders, analyses, and yet again further orders, all with a view to making it possible to allow the Kosovo Verification Mission to implement their tasks properly, that is to say to make it possible for the representatives of NATO and the OSCE to carry out their duties and responsibilities based on the agreement with OSCE and NATO in the field of verification in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the composition of this team, what can you say about that in terms of organisational units?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: We see 13 people here, but it actually consisted of 15 persons. We can see, if we look at the composition of the team, that the two top people of the team were persons who held the rank of assistant Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. The team also consisted of representatives of the first administration, specifically Lazic is a border expert. Then also all the branches and services as embodied in the General Staff, that is to say the ground forces, the air force, and anti-aircraft defence sector, then the intelligence administration, information and moral guidance, et cetera. You can see that these were people who were professionals in their respective fields. I wish to note that several people from this team had been military attachés of Yugoslavia in various countries in the world and that several people had experience in working with peacekeeping organisations with UNPROFOR, KFOR, SFOR, et cetera. So these were professionals. And you can also see what importance was attached to this team on the basis of the fact that the Chief of General Staff appointed two of his assistant chiefs, that is to say, General Obradovic, who was the team leader; and General Panic, who was deputy team leader. Then there was a secretary, it was Mr. Strunjac, but he was ill, so I often stood in for him. So I took part in the work of this team even more actively.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've given us an exhaustive answer, but now I would like to know, in relation to your basic duty, how did the fact that you were appointed to this team affect your regular job?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: At first we were all volunteers, if I can put it that way, on this team. That is to say that this was an additional duty that we discharged. So we carried out these duties and obligations in addition to our regular duties. However, after the team was appointed, all of us became busier and busier in relation to the team, and we did our regular jobs less and less. So our colleagues took over our work in our respective administrations. Later on, we were almost exclusively devoted to the tasks entrusted to this team.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I see that this liaison team was supposed to liaise with OSCE and NATO missions. Could you explain that to us. What was the field of work of this team?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The team was called precisely that way, liaison with the OSCE and NATO missions, because there were two basic agreements, that is to say, there was one agreement that was called the agreement between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the OSCE mission that was signed by Mr. Geremek, who was chairman-in-office in the OSCE at the time, and Mr. Jovanovic, who was foreign minister of Yugoslavia at the time. Then there was yet another agreement with the NATO mission that had been signed by General Clark from NATO and Mr. Perisic, Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. That is to say that there were two different agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this team actually enforce both agreements?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and equally so, that is to say, we carried out both duties in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Later on we will go back to this other agreement with NATO, but I would like to ask you something else. How did this team organise its work?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The team organised work round the clock, 24 hours a day; that is to say non-stop. In the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, we were given separate premises, and it was fully technically equipped, I mean our offices were. So we had the ability to communicate non-stop amongst ourselves, then with our respective administrations, and most importantly we had the possibility of communicating with the teams that existed in the armies, corps, and even up to the level of liaison officers who were in different garrisons in Kosovo and in the border battalions in Kosovo and Metohija. We held daily meetings, and we also had these briefings, that is to say, daily briefings where we analysed the situation every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you for your comment regarding paragraph 3 of this document. It is on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 2 both in B/C/S and in English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean where it says that the liaison team shall draw up the instructions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we drew up these instructions on the work and organisation of the team. In those instructions we --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. So in this way you were given that task?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you adopt these instructions?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. First the instructions and then the guide-lines on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Fine. We'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Honours, could I please tender this document first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before, I notice in the last paragraph - and it repeats something earlier in the document - there's no mention of the 1st Army. Is that significant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so because there was no need for a team in the 1st Army because the 1st Army had its headquarters in Belgrade, and it was not -- and the verification mission, rather, was not engaged in the territory of the 1st Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00589, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have document D006-1352.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That is number 2 in your binder, Mr. Novakovic. What we have here is a report dated the 2nd of March of the command of the 52nd -- 57th Border Battalion sent to the liaison team of the Pristina Corps. Mr. Novakovic, would that illustrate the implementation of these orders in depth, the orders of the Chief of General Staff of the 22nd of October? Could you please explain a bit how this actually functioned, the reporting that is?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe we should have mentioned earlier that teams at the Army of Yugoslavia in addition to this team in the General Staff had also, as the President noticed, teams in the 2nd Army, 3rd Army, in the air force, and anti-aircraft defence. Furthermore, in the 3rd Army the main team was in the Pristina Corps, and liaison officers were practically in garrisons that had their bases in brigade commands, Pristina, Djakovica, Urosevac, and Pec, and in border battalions. And in the air force and anti-aircraft defence, the teams were at corps level in the commands. There was no team, for instance, in the 1st Army or in the navy. So that was the system of liaison teams in depth. And since we had daily communications and we also had certain obligation -- obligations towards the OSCE and NATO missions, we needed to report to the missions; but in the same way, liaison teams reported to us about the implementation of tasks owed to the NATO and OSCE missions. So here we see a report from the liaison officer from the 57th Border Battalion, and this report speaks about the visit of OSCE representatives to his unit, or rather, the units of the 57th Border Battalion, the border units covered by that battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me just follow-up on the question posed by the President. In this team that was organised, this team had to liaise with both NATO and the OSCE verification mission. In view of this second agreement with NATO, which strategic group was responsible for NATO?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Our team was responsible, but also the strategic group of the air force and anti-aircraft defence. If you noticed, perhaps, I mentioned that Mr. Marjanovic was part of our team, but otherwise he was chief of administration for the air force and anti-aircraft defence in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. He is the officer who signed the memorandum of understanding with NATO on the one hand and the air force on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is that the reason why there were no representatives of the 1st Army on this team?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were not needed, as the navy was not needed on the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, although here we are already in March, we see that a delegation had arrived from the Kosovo Verification Mission to the border area. Could you give me your brief comment on the second and third paragraphs of the report. It begins with: "I was told they are able to provide ..." in the end of the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to mention that in these communications with the missions there were almost no problems with the NATO mission, and there were no major problems with the verification of the situation at the border, either on the border itself or behind the lines of the border. There were certain problems concerning entry and exit. It was said that a seven-day plan should be submitted, because the resolution itself says that border units may be inspected at request and the request had to come from the verification mission. So the verification mission didn't have to make any major effort; it simply had to notify its intention to visit. However, nobody was able to move around there without permission, not even an officer of the VJ. You had to notify your arrival primarily for security reasons. You had to be protected. Notification could be 24 hours in advance, but even shorter in order to organise access, as it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what does the third paragraph say about the position of the KVM?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: There were no particular issues concerning the border, and they did not point out any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please look at the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: They had no questions regarding the border or -- is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, the next one.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The meeting was also attended by Major Slobodan Spasic --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, no. This paragraph that begins with: "Their attention was drawn ..."

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, their attention was drawn --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You don't have to read aloud. Just comment on the last part of that sentence.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the representative of mission said that in future all visits would be announced, like all other entries to the border belt. He agreed with the liaison officer, and I believe that after that there were no further problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now please look at the last paragraph. "On return" or "after returning ..." It's the fifth line from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite a few problems on this issue. When they returned, another team was requested. I have to tell you that at one point when the mission was well established, in five regional centres they were able to have five different teams, five different patrols. So if it's five times 50, that meant 250 liaison officers were needed at any one time to follow the work of the verification mission. And we always thought that this activity should be co-ordinated because these liaison officers couldn't keep up and we didn't have many of these people who were able to follow-up on the work of the mission. There were delays, there were misunderstandings that shouldn't have occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I tender this document now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the document has already been admitted as Exhibit D00577.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I thank the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, you heard their comment. You need to speak more slowly, and I will try to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can I ask for D006-1434.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Your number 3, Mr. Novakovic. This is a regular weekly report of the command of the 3rd Army in its liaison team with both missions dated 24 December, 1999 [sic], addressed to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. Mr. Novakovic, did you receive such reports, and how did you proceed after receiving them?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we in the team -- on the team of the General Staff received such weekly reports regularly, and we also regularly received daily reports. On the basis of these reports, specifically this weekly one, and based on reports made available by the command of the air force and anti-aircraft defence, we, the team members, wrote up our own weekly report. And through the federal government's commission, that report would be submitted to the NATO and OSCE mission every week.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We see it's a very voluminous report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to see page 4 in English and page 5 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you comment on this paragraph that begins with the words "On the same day ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I mention, Mr. Djurdjic, page 14, line 24, you quoted the date as the 24th of December, 1999. If you look at the original and look at the content of the document, I think clearly the date was 24th of December, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As usual, you're right, Your Honour. I was reading too fast and I was told to slow down. But the document is from the 24th December, 1998. But even more precisely it says regular weekly report from the period of the 18th until 24th December. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, we said page 5. This paragraph that begins with the words "On the same day ..."

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this report speaks a lot about contacts on that day and other days, so with the representatives of the two missions. And we see in this paragraph that the gentleman from the mission, in this case probably members of KDOM, had not been announced. And they were told to speak to the liaison officer first and try to resolve their problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Whose representative was it? It's in the second line.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Someone from the British embassy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, a member of the mission of --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but he was temporary attaché with the British embassy, and by that time the KDOM was supposed to integrate with the mission. In any case, he was told what he needed to do because there were no liaison officers around and nobody could escort him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see page 6, that's 5 in English. I'd like you to look at -- I can't see it in English and I can't see the B/C/S either. Page 5 in English, further down, please. Towards the bottom. That's the Serbian. Can we now see the same thing in English. No, I still can't see it. It's section 2, page 5, in English. That's just above subheading "proposals" I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, did you have a look at this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The one that begins with: "On 24 December ..."

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you give us your comment regarding the procedure of verification?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were problems about this and they were not isolated problems. They cropped up quite often. Namely, liaison officers sometimes insisted on certain other issues and there were problems when they were supposed to go out into the field to verify an incident. I don't mean to say that the main task of the mission was the verification of incidents and cease-fires. We see here that the member of this team did not go out into the field to verify, and that incident had not been verified at that time. Later, perhaps, but not at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what was our position concerning the verification of cease-fire, and what did we propose, if anything?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: We were always pushing the idea - and I think we were right - that a protocol, an aide-memoire, should be drawn up and that the principle should be followed that each incident should be followed by writing up a protocol to be signed by both sides so that later there would be no manipulation with reports. Because it sometimes happened that everyone is in agreement while they are in the field and they note the same situation, both the mission and the VJ representatives, but as the report went further up, we realised that the ultimate report looked quite differently. So by the time the report was finalised by the mission, it was quite different. That's why we insisted on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We see that the Yugoslav Army had formed a team. Could you tell us something, if you know, that at the level of the country, the FRY, a team was also set up for relations with the KVM, and what was the relation between these two teams?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that. As I noted at the beginning, I know that at the level of the federal state there was a commission, and that commission was the main body in Yugoslavia in terms of co-operation with the OSCE and NATO missions. At the head of this commission was the vice premier in the federal government, I think it was Mr. Sainovic. And the commission comprised a number of ministers. But what was important for us from the army was that Defence minister and the Chief of General Staff were, by virtue of their positions, also members of this commission. Specifically, during 1998, it was General Perisic. And once General Ojdanic was appointed Chief of General Staff, he was a member of that team, that is to say, the commission. However, in both cases and throughout the time during which the commission existed, they were replaced by General Milorad Obradovic in the commission. He was an assistant to the Chief of General Staff, and for us it was important that he was heading the team of the Yugoslav Army General Staff. So through our head we had within the team a direct liaison and contacts with the Federal Commission. So to cut a long story short, in addition to the Federal Commission I know that there were also federal bodies, working groups, within the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Federal Ministry of the Interior, that is to say, within the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Novakovic, could you tell us what were the legal documents on the basis of which the team of the Yugoslav Army worked?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav Army team was working on the basis of the order of the Chief of General Staff. Actually, when we were discussing this team and the commission a while ago, what was our relation? The relation was professional, and the commission was not superior to our team. The team was based within the General Staff. And even though we had our own team leader, our main superior was always the Chief of General Staff. This is why I emphasise that we were working on the orders of the Chief of the General Staff. However, it is important that these orders followed from the obligations, that is to say, the agreement, with the OSCE mission, the agreement with the NATO mission, the agreement of -- about subregional control of weapons, as well as documents concerning diplomatic relations and so on. I cannot remember the specific names now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see P1074. And before that, I tender exhibit which was already in evidence, D006-1434.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is the report of the 24th of December, 1998. That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00590.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, in your binder under tab 4, it's P1074, it is Resolution 1160 dating March 1998, a resolution of the UN Security Council. So, Mr. Novakovic, it is page 3 in both versions, and let us focus on item 10 in the end of it. Could you please comment on the end of this item, 10, and tell us, as for your team and the relations with the missions, what did this mean?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, when I said what were the documents on the basis of which we were working, I had forgotten to note that our orders were also drawn up, of course, on the basis of all resolutions of UN Security Council, beginning with 1160, 1199, and all the others that followed. And as for this item 10 here, we can see that the resolution stresses the importance of the implementation of the agreement on subregional arms control, signed in Florence. We can see the year as well. This is important because the lack of understanding of this issue caused some problems with the representatives of the KVM because apart from the fact that they were not in charge of that, they very often insisted that they should implement the control from this agreement. And we can see that somebody else was in charge of implementing the agreement as it was until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please get D469 on the screen. This is the agreement on subregional arms control signed in Florence in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That is number 5 in your binder, Mr. Novakovic. And the resolution refers to this agreement and its implementation. And what was the substance of this agreement on control in terms of the control procedures?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The substance was that all the interested countries, that is to say, the countries of the former Yugoslavia, could at any given time request to examine the situation as regards the weapons, I think everything over the calibre 12.7 millimetres, that is to say, heavy weapons. And I have to stress that there were never any problems in connection with this. Even on one occasion at a meeting that I attended with the Chief of General Staff when he received Mr. Drewienkiewicz who was the deputy of the head of the mission, Mr. Drewienkiewicz expressed himself in very positive terms about the implementation of the obligations following from the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in the control procedures which were set out in this agreement. And the control was implemented in accordance with this agreement?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was implemented, and there were no problems at all as I said. And this procedure was continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see D160.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's number 6 in your binder, Mr. Novakovic. This is Resolution 1199, dated 23rd of September, 1998, a Security Council Resolution. And if we could please see what it says under item 1 on page 2, if you could please comment on what was requested by the UN Security Council in this resolution.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: We can see here that the first request was that all groups and individuals immediately cease hostilities. So the cease-fire was the basic task of the Kosovo Verification Mission, to note that there was a cease-fire and also to record any incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see the next page of this document and look at item 4(b).

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If you could please comment on that.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have to say that there were different opinions about how to interpret this item, and that was precisely where some problems arose and there were even tensions, especially this issue including access and complete freedom of movement of such monitors to, from, and within Kosovo, unimpeded, et cetera, et cetera, there were no problems. However, the mission representatives continually interpreted this item as if it meant accessing military facilities and barracks. And I have to say this was, throughout the period of our co-operation, one of the major problems. We believed that this did not automatically mean that they were at liberty to enter any military facility or barracks, because finally there were no incidents there that needed to be verified. And we have seen that the subregional arms control was in charge of controlling all the arms, and the OSCE was provided with lists of weapons in every period, annually. We also provided the Kosovo Verification Mission with that. But to cut the long story short, throughout this period I think that the only real tension was caused by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall revisit this issue later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the Exhibit P835.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And that's tab 7 in your binder, Mr. Novakovic. This is the agreement on the OSCE Kosovo Verification Mission signed by Mr. Geremek as the OSCE chairman and Mr. Zivadin Jovanovic as the foreign minister of FRY on the 16th of October, 1998. Mr. Novakovic, we have already said, but let us look at Roman numeral I, item 1, could you just briefly tell us what is envisaged there.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The verification mission will be established in accordance with the UN Security Council Resolution, and the FRY agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't have to say anything further. Now I'm interested in item 5, and what is the information you have about the implementation of this particular item?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. First there was an observation mission, that was the KDOM, and it worked on behalf of the OSCE mission. But once the verification mission was fully established, then the KDOM would be absorbed by it. I think it is well-known that the representatives of KDOM were actually representatives of NATO countries and some other countries who were mostly military attachés and their assistants and deputies. Some countries even had 30 or 40 and at the end even 120 representatives. And I must say at the beginning that they noted the situation, they had access to everything; but I know that even after the mission was established, some of them remained outside of the mission. They were not members of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And as for item 6?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was noted that the FRY government guaranteed safety and security, and I think that there were no problems regarding this issue. But we shall see that there were some problems when individual members or even top figures within the mission expressed concern, but I think that in military terms this would be called stoking up the situation. I think that there were no problems -- not that I think. I know that there were no problems in terms of incidents caused by FRY representatives with mission representatives. Of course there were some minor incidents because not everything is ideal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please have a look at the Roman numeral II on the next page of the document you have in front of you. And if we could see, again, item 1 in that section.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Novakovic, did you ever receive reports of the Kosovo Verification Mission during their stay in the FRY?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, that was agreed on, but really we had no feedback. That is to say, we did not receive any reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a look at section beginning with the Roman numeral III and item number 1. It's on the same page in English. If we could just scroll down, please. It is at the bottom of the page, the last item.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see that. It is emphasised here, because it was the most important task, that the mission would travel throughout Kosovo and verify whether all the parties were honouring the cease-fire, that it would request reports on the cease-fire, and again the issue of the freedom of movement and access to various places.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, was the emphasise of the mission to verify the cease-fire considering the reports that you received, and was freedom of movement and freedom of access something that was allowed to them in accordance with this agreement?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was not implemented that way. We can see and note that the main task was to record cease-fire -- now I cannot say that it was not the main task, but that was not always the focus of their activities, as I said. Very often they would rather focus on facilities, access to facilities, and that was something they kept insisting on. And as for freedom of movement, they had absolute freedom of movement except for entry to barracks, even though concessions were made even in that sense. According to some agreements the representatives of the mission were allowed to enter barracks without any major problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, considering the differing interpretations of the provisions of the agreement, which are obvious from what you said, were there any proposals that were sent to the mission about how to overcome this?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, our people at the lower levels in the teams of various armies and corps, and even from our main team and from the Federal Commission, had some proposals. They would say, Well, gentlemen, please could we use the diplomatic channels and propose to resolve this issue, specifically this issue of entry to the barracks? However, there was no understanding on the part of the mission representatives because General Drewienkiewicz would always say, No, this issue is resolved for us. We can enter any barracks whenever we want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd like to have a look at the next page, please --, or rather, we already do have that page in English, but could we just see the right page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So tell me, did the FRY honour its obligation to send weekly information?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. We already commented on that in relation to another document a few minutes ago. We received reports primarily from the team from the 3rd Army and also from the air force and anti-aircraft defence. We compiled the report. I think it was on Tuesday usually. And we sent our report to the federal government, and the federal government sent it to the Kosovo Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at paragraph 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell us, is that the part of the agreement that you talked about when you spoke about the border belt? So it is your page 3, number 4.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So the mission shall maintain liaison with FRY authorities concerning border control activities and movements by units with border control responsibilities through areas of Kosovo away from the border. So these are in-depth security units. And when invited by the FRY authorities and upon its request, the verification mission will visit border control units and accompany them as they perform their normal border control roles, so there was no problem whatsoever. They could accompany them when they were exercising control at the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But we see here that what was envisaged was to act upon their request?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let us translate this into practical terms. To whom were they supposed to submit such a request?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a written request, specific application of any kind. They were just supposed to tell the liaison officer, We will come tomorrow; we will come within the next five days; we will come in a month's time. Quite simply, we were so flexible that we -- I mean, I say "we," but I mean that it was people on the ground. It was easier to work that way, quite simply to announce that during the next few days, for instance, the members of the mission will be on the ground. Because in that area, in that belt, no one was allowed to move about except for the population living there. Our officers could not move there without permission either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In practice, what did KVM members do in relation to this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: In practice, I don't know why this was the case, but often there were situations when they would come unannounced and then they wanted to intervene immediately. They said that they didn't have enough time. They wanted to engage in verifications straightaway. But the problem was that we did not have enough liaison officers, especially not in the first part. Let me try to explain this in two specific sentences: This liaison officer could have been, say, a commander of a border company, and he could have been at a particular border post, X, for instance. And then they, the verifiers, appear at border post Y. So there can be, say, two hours required for him to get from border post X to border post Y. I am not very familiar with the border, but the people who are very knowledgeable know that it wasn't all that readily accessible and it wasn't really easy to negotiate these difficult areas. Also, it was a question related to the personal security and safety of the verifiers. They were supposed to be escorted and guarded while touring the border area. We saw that our country did take upon itself to provide security for the verifiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like us to move on to the next page, please, Roman numeral IV, number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This agreement envisaged the 2.000 unarmed verifiers from OSCE member countries will be there. Mr. Novakovic, to the best of your knowledge, these unarmed verifiers, what were they, professionally?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that first and foremost the OSCE mission was supposed to be a civilian mission. As for the verifiers, over 90 per cent of them were officers. We knew some of these people from contacts that we had in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Suffice it to say that the deputy chief of mission was a general, and he introduced himself that way in public. Then there were a few other generals and colonels and officers at different levels. So practically this was a civilian mission consisting of professional soldiers, of military officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a team, were you aware of the problems related to the personal weapons of the members of the KVM?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not directly, but there was some information to the effect that they asked to use weapons. But it was clearly stated here that they were supposed to be unarmed, so we could not accept that. I repeat that our country had the obligation to protect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know, perhaps, of some requests pertaining to helicopters, requests that were made to the organs for co-operation with KVM?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Helicopters were mentioned, I think, for medical purposes. And we, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, made an offer. We did not have enough helicopters. The military medical academy and our medical service in general could have handled that obligation on their own too. And in the agreement there was no mention of the use of any helicopters that were not owned by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have document P837, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's number 8 for you, Mr. Novakovic. This is a record from a meeting held on the 25th of October, 1998, that was signed by Mr. Nikola Sainovic, General Vlastimir Djordjevic, General Klaus Naumann, and General Wesley Clark. I would like to ask you, Mr. Novakovic, in relation to paragraph 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we actually have the next page, please, if possible in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Have you seen it, Mr. Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I looked at paragraph 4 and --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you now look at paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to move on to the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, we see here that the FRY, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is to say, the federal government and the republican governments, took upon themselves an obligation that they would meet by 1200 hours on the 27th of October, 1998, and they would notify KDOM thereof. And by 1200 hours on the 29th of October, they will be informed about the new structures and numbers. I would be interested in hearing whether we met these obligations?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can say that that is the case. After these agreements - and we do know what preceded this agreement - the FRY met these requests and acted in accordance with paragraph 7. That is to say that the units were out of Kosovo and Metohija except for these groups as stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We did not go into the political and security situation in the beginning of October 1998, but I would like to ask you about the consequences if obligations from the agreement were not met, in view of the preceding situation that is.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, there was a looming danger of NATO bombing, and that threat unfortunately was materialised several months later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at paragraph 5 now, please. That states the units that were allowed to stay outside the border belt. I would like to know whether these -- this agreement and these obligations that were taken forbade the training activities of the units of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. We see that as far as these three units are concerned, there weren't any serious problems in relation to verification. Sometimes the question of personnel levels was raised, but I think it was a minor issue, not really noteworthy. We saw in the agreement and in our reporting obligations that we were supposed to include in our reports the entry of units into Kosovo and Metohija, their departure from Kosovo and Metohija, and their movement within the boundary of Kosovo and Metohija. That is to say, if a unit moved about outside Kosovo and Metohija, that was possibly for supplies or some intervention if a unit had been attacked. For the most part, units moved about for training purposes. So training was not forbid, even more so because very often units were supposed to be replaced. Units could stay in Kosovo for three months after completing training. I'm referring to soldiers. So a group of soldiers needs to be brought into Kosovo, then returned, and the ones who did come in were young soldiers, relatively young, who had just completed their training. So they were supposed to receive additional training there in the field where they were supposed to be. So I emphasise that the training of soldiers and officers was allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Roman numeral III, please, the last sentence. Can you give us your comment on that. How did the commission apply this part of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was stated very clearly that the units of the Army of Yugoslavia, in accordance with the right to self-defence, retained the right to respond adequately and proportionately. The question of this proportionate response, very often in theory and in practice there is reference to excessive use of force in case of terrorist actions. It is hard to define that particular issue, whether the commander at a given point in time can assess on the spot which force he is going to use to respond. That's a different matter altogether. The important thing is that at a given point in time a unit of the Army of Yugoslavia had the right to respond adequately and proportionately to any form of terrorist activity or a violation of law that could jeopardise lives and safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter document 00454. It's a Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is tab 9 in your binder. Mr. Novakovic, this is an agreement between NATO and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. You told us that your team was tasked with co-operating with this NATO mission as well on the basis of the decision that we've already seen. So that is the agreement of the 15th of October, 1998. Tell me, to the best of your knowledge, how was this agreement carried out?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: This agreement was carried out practically without any problems whatsoever. Perhaps I can put it this way: There were three important tasks there, that is to say, verification and requests to exercise control over the air-space above Kosovo and Metohija and the joint zone of security which is 25 kilometres away from the so-called administrative border of Kosovo and Metohija. The second group of tasks was the control of integrated systems of air defence, that is to say, the air defences that were in Kosovo and Metohija were grouped in particular locations, garrisons, so that they could be under control. And the third group of tasks on the basis of this agreement related to command over this air-space control. And this command was carried out from two centres, namely, the centre at the command of the air force and air defence of the Army of Yugoslavia, specifically in Zemun, and there were three NATO officers present at that centre. The other centre was the centre of the Joint Command, which I cannot remember its exact name right now. That was in Vicenza in Italy, and three air force officers of the Army of Yugoslavia were present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This was military verification; right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, military verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You said there were no problems, but did the Kosovo Verification Mission, to the best of your knowledge, attempt to exercise the kind of control regulated by this agreement that we're looking at now?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were a number of such attempts, and they created problems because we thought they shouldn't be doing that, considering that the issue had been quite adequately resolved by our agreement with NATO. And that's how representatives of the mission were able to get information from their colleagues in NATO at any time. That's one thing. And second, they were not in charge of controlling these systems, although we did, as a sign of goodwill and co-operation, we did allow them a couple of times to look even at these systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened with these systems that were reviewed by the Kosovo Verification Mission during the aggression?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can give you some indicators. It speaks volumes that these systems were destroyed among the first at the beginning of the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I tender this document now, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00591.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have now the first break and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, just for the record, we need to clear up certain things. It is -- you are recorded as saying: "We did not have ... helicopters." And then you spoke about helicopters by the military medical academy that were offered.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I said that the agreement did not mention any helicopters in relation to the mission, but we had helicopters. And since medical issues were being discussed, I said that the military medical academy with its teams could provide medical services and the air force had helicopters, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was able to deal with the issue quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the mission accept this offer made by the FRY with regard to the use of its helicopters?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You said the agreement did not envisage any helicopters for the civilian verification mission, but were any steps taken to amend the agreement by the Kosovo Verification Mission, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Not that I know of. They did not propose any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, could you now move to document in tab 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may I ask for D006-1447.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you first, this team of the General Staff of the VJ for the implementation of agreements with NATO and the OSCE, did it produce any documents so that this could be implemented on lower levels of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've already mentioned we made the basic document called instructions. We also made one instruction, one draft protocol, and a draft aide-memoire. We also produced a draft joint protocol and a couple of more suggestions. If teams at lower levels required anything from us, we made it available to them either verbally or in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind all your activities and the documents we've just mentioned as being basic documents, how did the VJ view its co-operation with the KVM?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that from the outset we had a relationship with NATO and the KVM that we took very seriously, and you will see that in our engagement of human resources and in the fact that we concentrated on our jobs related to the team at the detriment of our regular jobs and that we created teams at lower levels of the VJ. And we made every effort to enable the best possible implementation of our agreements with NATO and the OSCE. To sum up, we did our best to enable the verification mission to do its job.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have before us a document called: Summary of obligations, tasks, implementation, and methodology of work ensuing from the agreement on the OSCE Kosmet Verification Mission, dated 16 October 1998. It was produced at the office of the federal minister of foreign affairs. It's your tab 11. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What can you say about this document? What were the VJ's obligations?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: This document issues a number of tasks to all the parties involved in the agreement with the mission. We see here the Federal Foreign Ministry, the Federal Ministry of the Interior, the Republic Ministry of the Interior, the Army of Yugoslavia also has certain obligations, as does the Ministry for Telecommunications, the Federal Ministry for Traffic and Transport, the Yugoslav Red Cross, and the Commission for Refugees. And then we have a table which states a number of tasks, indicating who is responsible --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please go on, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: One task for the Army of Yugoslavia is to guarantee the security and safety of the OSCE mission, to co-operate in the mission's evacuation in case of emergency, to co-ordinate and provide support to the authorities and members of the mission, to provide medical services through the military medical academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe we can move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then the Army of Yugoslavia is under obligation to provide access to the airport in Belgrade, to produce reports on the situation and the movement of forces, to maintain contacts regarding the inspection of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: All these are specific tasks that were elaborated later in separate documents. Here they are just listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you explain the relationship of this team for liaison with NATO and OSCE and the other agencies listed here. What were their links like in practice?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as VJ is concerned, we had a vertical system of communication. At the top was the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, lower come teams of the armies --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, I mean with other agencies.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: We did the co-ordination of this co-operation, but we were not subordinated in relation to the Federal Commission. All these other agencies, such as ministries, had horizontal links. They had parallel Working Groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about the teams at lower levels of the VJ, did they have co-ordination points in Pristina in order to co-operate with similar bases of other authorities?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Just as we had a team in the VJ, they had appropriate communications with their own agencies at higher levels. Teams in armies and at corps level also had horizontal links with appropriate authorities on the ground. There was a co-ordination body specifically in Pristina, and they had direct links with that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00592, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, please go back now to tab 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I kindly request document D006-1483.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is an instruction on the relations between the VJ on the one hand and OSCE and NATO missions on the other hand for verification in Kosovo and Metohija dated 20th October, 1998, adopted by the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ, Lieutenant-General Momcilo Perisic. Can you tell us, Mr. Novakovic, about the nature of this document, how it came to be, and how it was implemented as far as the VJ is concerned?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: This is an instruction, a fundamental document, that instructs all the other parties involved, including our team, which issues they will be dealing with. First of all, there are general provisions invoking the documents that underlie this co-operation, such as the resolutions and agreements. It also says that it does not affect our sovereignty, that the mission has the approval of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that enjoys -- it enjoys diplomatic immunity --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Look at para 2. I would like your comment on the last sentence in para 2: "Armed attacks against individuals and installations of the VJ, the combat rules of engagement ..."

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: We have already seen the right of self-defence and response to terrorist attacks in one of the basic documents. We believed that this should also be included in this basic document, and it is indeed included in this first chapter. We attached special importance to it, and we wanted it in the first chapter. And we also wanted to invoke combat rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is this also envisaged by the Rules of Service of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Primarily combat rules, rules of engagement. But also in the laws and the constitution of the FRY and the constitutions of some other countries in that period, the army's defined, saying the army is to protect sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the constitutional order. So the protection of the constitutional order is one of the duties of the army. It was written on the Law on Defence and the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: If I may continue, I won't be too long. In the second part, the document speaks of the duties of the mission, the co-operation at the level of the 3rd Army and the command of the air force, the team in Vicenza is mentioned. It elaborates co-operation at the level of the anti-aircraft defence and mentions the team at the level of the Pristina Corps and the level of garrisons. It also mentions liaison officers and auxiliary personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: About liaison officers, what kind of profile was required? What were the duties of liaison officers at the beginning, and how did they develop over time?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: There is a great difference between the initial period and later periods. These people were taken from unit commands, such as battalions and brigades and border battalions. Some of these were officers or commanding officers who had what was needed, such as basic knowledge of foreign language. But as time went on, we found other people who had a more perfect command of English. And in the last stage, when we were preparing a workshop, we brought in a group of 20 men whose exclusive task was to be liaison officers. They had good English; they were experienced; and they were able to work in shifts, 24 hour/7 and be at the disposal of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, at this last stage you had liaison officers who had no other job?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was their only duty. They had been brought in from other organisational units of the General Staff, and they were given temporary appointments as liaison officers. But we also kept on the previous liaison officers. So the number of liaison people increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please turn to page 6 now, page 6 in both versions, please. That's in chapter 2 under (a).

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, it says: "By submitting reports to the OSCE verification missions ..." Did your team members fulfil this obligation, and how did they do that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think I have noted this twice already, that on receiving reports from the teams, primarily from the 3rd Army, the air force, and anti-aircraft defence, we would collate these reports and then we would send them to the mission through the Federal Commission once a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And under (g)?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean this, following the mission?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: You can see here that we fulfilled all the elementary duties from the agreements with the missions of OSCE and NATO and the resolutions. This is a document that was written at the beginning, so some things are repeated, but we were maybe too extensive in our descriptions. But we say here that we would escort the representatives from the OSCE mission during their movements in the border zone, during their visits of border units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I see here that in spite of such detailed instructions, in the attachment that you also submitted all the basic documents which obliged the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, all the resolutions and the agreements that we have discussed, so that they could directly read these documents, those who used the instructions?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did that. And all our associates, I mean, all the teams and liaison officers were sent all the documents as well as all other guide-lines so that we would educate them as well as possible. And I should say that, on one occasion, we made a study in which we included all the documents that we mentioned as well as others. And on one occasion when there was a meeting of the Chief of General Staff, and I think General Perisic was the chief at the time, we gave this study, it was a whole book, to General Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00593.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see D006-1502.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 12, Mr. Novakovic, and it is Defence number 76, that's the Defence number. We'll see it on the screen in a second. These are notes from the meeting between the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, Dragoljub Ojdanic, and the deputy chief of the OSCE mission in Kosovo and Metohija, Major-General John Drewienkiewicz. The notes are dated the 15th of December, 1998, and the meeting was held on the 27th of November, 1998. Mr. Novakovic, did you attending this meeting between General Drewienkiewicz and General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I attended the meeting. And that can be seen from footnote number 1, which lists the members, those who attended the meeting, and my name is included there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what was the atmosphere in which this meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me say that it was protocolary atmosphere. At the beginning I think that around this time General Ojdanic had been appointed Chief of General Staff, and General Drewienkiewicz asked to be received by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 2 of this document in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is at the top of the page in B/C/S, Mr. Novakovic, the section where General Drewienkiewicz promised that the work of the mission will be open and that he would submit reports of the mission to the Yugoslav Army 72 hours after the verification at the latest. Can you please explain this for us and how this was implemented?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the mission did not submit such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any attempts to obtain such reports?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Through General Obradovic, who was our representative in the commission, we requested that such reports be submitted. However, there was no reaction to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we can see in the next paragraph the procedures with the so-called KLA are mentioned. Can you tell us what was the position of the mission in relation to the Kosovo Liberation Army during their stay in the territory of FRY?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: There were many requests and tasks and comments expressed at this meeting, but General Drewienkiewicz really expressed the position that the procedure would be the same with the so-called KLA. And as far as I know, the political agreement was never reached, at least I do not know that it was reached between the mission on the one hand and the KLA on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now look at the paragraph where General Obradovic and Marjanovic are mentioned. Could we comment on this part of the notes about the methodology of conducting verification, if you could expand a little bit on this?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: General Ojdanic acted on the information about the work of the mission, which he received, and he emphasised that the VJ was ready to honour all the provisions from the resolution, that it would submit reports. I said that we did submit them. But he also asked if the reports that we submit to the mission would be identical to the reports that the mission submitted to OSCE, because there were some indications that they were not exactly the same. We could understand that this was professionally processed and so on. General Obradovic requested -- maybe not to force, I don't think he used that term, but to make sure that the political leadership of the Kosovo Albanians be placed -- place the so-called KLA under control, because there were some indications that these terrorist forces - as we called them in our speech - were not under control. And he was interested in the methods of work. And it was precisely in terms of the methods that we proposed to create a protocol. And on behalf of our team, the person who was in charge of drafting the protocol was Colonel Marjanovic with a group of other people, and he also talked about the protocol. However, General Drewienkiewicz was skeptical. He said that he had no time for such a protocol, that it would take a lot of time. However, it was possible to draw it up in a day or two. So it was not true that much time was needed for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: As for the information, you see in the last paragraph, General Drewienkiewicz says that they requested information about weapons, and number of troops should be submitted to the mission so that they would know what to verify. Was this the information that had already been submitted; and if yes, to whom and how, and were there any later procedures relating to this on part of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have to say that at the beginning of the meeting, General Drewienkiewicz expressed satisfaction and said that the Yugoslav Army was appropriately submitting reports in terms of the subregional arms control, that he had no objections, that he had already watched a film on how to do that, and that he had no objections relating to that. However, he said that he wished to receive such a report as well, because he expressed the position that the KVM mission was also entitled to control the heavy weapons systems, which is not in the agreement. Further, we told General Drewienkiewicz that he could receive the report from NATO representatives, that is to say, from the Kosovo Diplomatic Mission, as they had already collected the information. And then the general said that he wished to receive it directly from the Yugoslav Army. And I know that within two or three days, around the 30th, we simply used the same information that we had submitted to OSCE. So now we took out the information relating to units stationed in Kosovo and Metohija and we submitted that to the Kosovo Verification Mission, also through the Federal Commission through which we would usually submit documents. So we did send the information to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please move to page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
