utterances.text: You already started talking about this. We see here General Obradovic and what he said.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I have already said, in terms of this agreement on subregional arms control, and there was this issue of entry to barracks that was raised here and it dominated the meeting. General Obradovic said that the issue was not regulated by the agreement and that this could not be done before a political decision was made and before the Chief of General Staff issued an order that would regulate that. And at a later stage of our relations, we will see that we had envisaged this possibility even though there was no political decision, that the Chief of General Staff could, on certain occasions, allow even this kind of verification, that would imply entry to barracks. And we really allowed that from time to time -- not frequently, but we did do it sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, we see here that this was a meeting between the deputy head of the Kosovo Verification Mission and the Chief of General Staff and this kind of response given to the deputy head of the Kosovo Verification Mission. Can you please tell us whether the General Staff was authorised to negotiate about amendments to the agreement on the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, absolutely not. You may note here that General Obradovic also said in one sentence that this could not be implemented until a political decision was made, and the order of the Chief of General Staff could not follow without a political decision. And on that occasion we also asked General Drewienkiewicz and other persons who were attending the meeting, there was a whole delegation, to raise this issue through the head of the mission, Mr. Walker, through appropriate diplomatic channels so that the issue be examined at the political levels, and then there would be no problems at all -- there shouldn't have been any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Novakovic, what I find interesting here, you already explained that General Ojdanic also said that the authorities were asked to provide an appropriate interpretation, that this was the way to do that, but this is what I find interesting. We have here a representative of the Kosovo Verification Mission. He has a very high position. He may be the second man. And he requests from us information that was already submitted to OSCE, that is to say, the organisation which set up the verification mission, which is a part of the OSCE system.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is peculiar, but you have seen that, in spite of that, General Ojdanic promised - and we really fulfilled that - that we would submit the information, and that as for other information we could not allow that without a political decision, not really information but allowing access to barracks and so on. Whatever else was at the level of the Yugoslav Army was resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is also mentioned here is the agreement on arms control, the subregional one, and the procedures, and that the Kosovo Verification Mission, as we can see here, wanted to control such arms as well. But what was provided in the agreement? How was the military control of arms to be conducted according to the subregional agreement?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was an appropriate announcement, I think 36 hours were needed, there would be an announcement, and at any moment it was possible for the interested parties to examine and as many times as they wished what they wanted to examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General Novakovic [as interpreted], did this agreement on subregional arms control then allow someone to come somewhere and say: I want to count the weaponry now?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Announcement was necessary. And even putting that aside, the Kosovo Verification Mission did not have the -- was not authorised to do that. We have looked at what the UN Security Council Resolution said and also what the agreement says; it remained in force, I mean the verification according to the subregional arms control. And the UN Security Council Resolution confirmed the importance of this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to what you know, did the members of the Kosovo Verification Mission wish not only to come directly to the border zone and enter facilities or barracks, but also to enter VJ barracks and facilities whenever they would show up there?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that happened frequently, and I already emphasised several times that that was the greatest problem and that that was where the misunderstandings happened. Some of the verifiers even behaved inappropriately. They almost wanted to enter by force through the guards. But they were officers and they knew that this was not possible. I don't know how they imagined that they could just pass by the guards. It was inappropriate in my view that a verifier should try to enter in that way. But there were such incidents, and we submitted reports on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00594.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have document D008-1553 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That is tab 13 in your binder, Mr. Novakovic. 481 is the Defence number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can I ask which question I'm supposed to repeat? Thank you. And if I need to repeat it, the number I said was D008-1553, and I think that we now have the right document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That is the order of the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia dated the 11th of December, 1998. It has to do with control and assistance to the 3rd Army with regard to relations with OSCE and NATO missions. Mr. Novakovic, can you tell us a bit more about this order?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the permission of the Honourable Trial Chamber, just two remarks. In view of this period from October 1998 until March 1999, I was in Kosovo three times on such missions. Once I was in a large group that was headed by the Chief of General Staff, and twice I was leader of this Working Group from the team, once on the basis of this order in December and another time in March when we organised a seminar. Now, what was the principle involved? We were viewing the way in which the Army of Yugoslavia had carried out its obligations until then, what needed to be resolved, and we, a work group, went to the actual area involved. We visited all the commands, units in the garrisons in Kosovo and Metohija, that is to say that we were in the corps command, in the brigade commands, the border battalions, and those three areas that were -- three units that were in the area. On the basis of that, we compiled a report. On the basis of the report, the Chief of General Staff wrote an order, on the basis of which we improved our work and resolved the problems involved. So this is the initial order on the basis of which we were authorised to go to the units of the Pristina Corps, I mean the Working Group. That would be it in the briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We see here that the date is the 11th of December, 1998, and now paragraph 2 says training through seminars. Tell me, how many training seminars were there after this 11th of December, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: We had several meetings, and the most important seminar was the one that was held in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll deal with that later. And now we see on page 4, or rather, page 3. We see the work-plan. We see that you're the person who wrote it up.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my colleagues and I. As you can see, it was the Chief of General Staff who signed the order, and the leader of our team, General Obradovic, approved this document. So during the course of those few days while we were there, we briefly outlined what we would do. The important thing is that we visited all the units concerned, the corps command, the brigade commands, and the commands of the border battalions. We had the opportunity of contacting the liaison team from the 3rd Army there, the one that was detached in Pristina. At that point, it was headed by General Tomislav Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00595.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have document D006-1563.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That is tab 14 for you, Mr. Novakovic, and it's Defence number 79. We see a report of the Work Group of the team, and it's sent to the General Staff. It has to do with relations with NATO -- the NATO mission. It was signed by Colonel Novakovic. It has to do with the implementation of the previous document, namely, the order of the 11th of December, 1998. Mr. Novakovic, you submitted this report. I would like us to comment upon paragraph 1, if you could tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the control that we carried out over those three days, we talked to several persons, namely, the command structure, that is to say, the commanders, and the representatives of the teams, first and foremost, the leaders of teams and liaison officers. We saw what the problems involved were. Then we wrote up a report and subsequently made proposals as to what we thought should be done. Here we are stating what the situation is. First of all we say that verification of the reported PVO, that is to say, verification in accordance with the agreement with NATO, was carried out in accordance with the agreed procedure, that is to say, the protocol that had been agreed upon, that it was carried out professionally, and that the situation on the ground corresponded to the reported one. A verification report was compiled in Serbian and English, it was signed for each verification, and what is pointed out here was the high level of co-operation on the part of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now hear your comments on paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that refers to the problem that we keep going back to. We don't want to say that everything was bad in relation to the OSCE mission, but there were quite a few problems involved because of their insistence not to announce their visits. That was the main problem. They said something more or less along the lines of: That is what we've been allowed to do on the basis of the Security Council Resolution and that is that. Perhaps there was nervousness on both sides because we could not always be very co-operative if we did not have a liaison officer nearby at a particular moment. But the basic point was that they insisted that this had to be done at all costs and without previous contacts and consultations, agreement. We will see that at all levels the teams had hundreds of meetings. There were tens of meetings held every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I see here in paragraph 3 that it is stated that the Kosovo Verification Mission was duly informed on time about incidents, and the command of the Pristina Corps required the verification of incidents, but in some instances the KVM verifiers refused to sign the verification reports. Can you tell us a bit more about that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the problems too, because when we have these discussions, we are actually presenting the problems as they were. The KVM did carry out its obligations on the basis of the agreement, but, indeed, we always insisted on having the report, the minutes, signed together. What our people saw and what the OSCE people saw, that had to be agreed upon so both parties could sign. However, some verification mission members did sign these reports and others thought that it wasn't necessary and they wouldn't, so that was the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We see here that there were no such problems with NATO. We see that in paragraph 1 in reference to air-space control, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at the next page now -- the English is fine, actually, paragraph 4 is here. But could we have the next page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you give us your comment on paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. We are stating here that liaison officers from those units are fully trained for the implementation of these tasks, and we just pointed out, yet again, this problem of the constant insistence on a protocol so that there would be a single approach. There were many members of the verification missions and many groups, and there weren't problems in our dealings with all of them, but there really was that problem of having a single protocol. Perhaps it did not have to be a single protocol, but there has to be a system that would be agreed upon. The representatives of the army and the KVM do not always have to agree on everything, but we insisted that it all be written in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to that, did you elaborate a methodology and did you offer it to the KVM in order to accept and carry out such a procedure?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We wrote up this protocol. It was Colonel Marjanovic who did that, but I also prepared a memo. However, throughout that period, it really depended on an independent decision taken by the verifier. The verifiers would individually say whether they wanted to sign it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about the procedure involved? We see the methodology. Did that actually -- was that fully carried out?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the verifiers involved. I don't really want to single anyone out on the basis of the state they originally came from, but it depended on how they carried out verification on the ground. Some of these people, some of the leaders of these verification teams, did have understanding and others did not. So that was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any information as to why some verifiers refused to apply such a procedure and for you to sign these reports?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, usually the answer was: That is not what the agreement says.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you gave proposals at the end of this document. Would you have anything to explain to us in relation to these proposals?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In this first proposal, we speak of the need to have this protocol and an appropriate methodology. Also, there is a reference to the Federal Commission, so we are asking for their position on this problem of accessing units. Also, there was this problem of minefields that existed only in the border belt. There weren't any in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija -- or at least the army had not created any minefields there. Then also there was the possibility of creating a separate administration which would make it more official than just a team.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Novakovic, we can read up on that. We can read it ourselves. If you have nothing to add to what was written here --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00596.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now ask for D006-1469.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's tab 15 for you, sir. This is an order from the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia dated 23rd December, 1998. I should like to ask you, Mr. Novakovic, to explain in simple terms.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: This is an order from the Chief of General Staff. It's giving a different shape to our observations from the ground when we went on a field mission and that we had submitted to our team leader that the Chief of the General Staff is now making this official. Again, he insists on the protocol and the methodology of verification. There was a problem with who was going to be the representative of the Army of Yugoslavia on the co-ordination team. We suggested this. And the Chief of the General Staff decided that it should be the team leader from the 3rd Army in Pristina, General Mladenovic. Furthermore, the Chief of the General Staff says that whenever possible liaison officers in garrisons and in border battalions should be relieved of other duties and focus on their work with the Kosovo Verification Mission. Also, he specifies that daily and weekly exchanges of information with the mission should take place, but only one weekly report should be written. Why? Because there had been this idea of writing a daily report to the missions, and at lower levels liaison officers were not really inclined to accept this. It was too much work, and it was not envisaged by the agreement anyway. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at para 6, sub-para 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the issue of entry into barracks. Verification in barracks, border posts, depots, except the anti-aircraft defence systems, are not to be accepted without special approval. When I say "border posts," that means entering the watch-tower itself, inspecting the personnel and their weapons. That requires a special approval from the Chief of the General Staff. And the Chief of the General Staff leaves open the possibility of giving access to barracks, regardless of political agreement to defuse tensions and display a sign of goodwill.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00597, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at D006-1457.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tab 16. It's a 65 ter number 72. That's an order of the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia dated 8 March 1999. Mr. Novakovic, explain this order, please, and tell me whether you had made any proposals about this to the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: This is already March 1999, and this is -- this was our best proposal, our best offer for regulating our relations with the mission -- with the missions. There is a reference to minor deficiencies and omissions, mainly at the lower level. I'm not trying to say that we at the higher level were better, but at lower levels people did have less experience. It was decided that one order should cover all these issues and specify what should be done better. I just need to say that a few days before this order we had made an analysis of our relationship and co-operation of the problems we had on our side and the KVM experienced, the sticking points; and we presented the results to our team. General Obradovic's team leader, and as assistant Chief of the General Staff, reported at a collegium meeting or directly to the Chief of the General Staff in this matter. And the Chief of the General Staff accepted most of our suggestions. And, on that basis, he gave us approval to prepare an order that he signed eventually, organisation of the work and relations between the VJ and the missions. I believe this is the last order of this kind. And one of the tasks given here specifies exactly what need -- what needs to be done at each level. This replaces all previous orders from the Chief of the General Staff, and there had been a dozen or so. We are now moving into a stage where, on the basis of this order, we're organising a workshop not for the sake of organising a workshop, but forming a group of 20 liaison officers who will have no other duties but this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I see it mentions some strategic groups and some changes in personnel, but I believe point 6 is interesting because it deals with the jurisdiction of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are no major changes, but it states where the team of the 3rd Army should be based. It used to be in a barracks and it's now relocated, but it gives more detail how liaison officers from the Pristina Corps need to be placed: Two officers in the corps command -- we're talking about these new officers, and it speaks of every garrison, Mitrovica, Pec, Djakovica, Prizren, Urosevac, two officers each in the brigade command and one officer per border battalion. That means 20 officers who are able to work 24/7 and be constantly at the disposal of both the VJ and the KVM, that is, both missions, the OSCE and NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00598.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now call D006-1560.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's your tab 17, 65 ter 78. We see another order of the Chief of the General Staff dated 8 March 1999, organising and conducting a seminar including team members and liaison officers. Could you explain this order?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said a few words about it. This is our crown achievement, our best result. And now we receive an order from the Chief of the General Staff to organise a seminar to work with team members and with liaison officers. Four or five colleagues from my team and myself were involved, and we spent four or five days there. We had contacts with the corps command, with brigade commands, and we organised - although I don't see the plan here - we organised this workshop in such a way that it was attended by all those who had served as liaison officers before; brigade commanders from the Pristina Corps were present on the first day; and there were 20 liaison officers in the rank of captain first class to colonel - I keep emphasising this - who travelled with me to Belgrade -- from Belgrade. And we educated all these people together with those who were already liaison officers. We presented the political and other bases for our work, we exchanged opinions, after that we had several hours of deliberations. But mainly, we showed how this verification should be done within units and on the border. I emphasise that we availed ourselves of this opportunity to include in this workshop representatives of the verification mission from OSCE. General Drewienkiewicz was present personally. We wanted him to see with our [as interpreted] own eyes what we were doing, and we gave him an opportunity to make an address to team members and liaison officers about -- I remember his particular slide, the things that cause anger --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we should interrupt the witness here in order to avoid certain problems we've had before. It's enough to know that he was involved. But if the Trial Chamber believes I should, I can allow the witness to tell us which topics were discussed. But perhaps to avoid problems, although I don't see any problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We don't need those details. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If you have anything else to say apart from Drewienkiewicz?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I meant to mention just a few words about the -- maybe I got carried away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Never mind. Mr. Novakovic, we see that this was on the 8th of March and the mission left the territory of the FRY in Kosovo and Metohija on the 20th. Could you tell us whether their departure took place in complete safety?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me add that this order was dated 8 March, but we had this workshop from the 10th to the 14th. And the mission were absolutely safe as they were leaving. There were never any security issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You told us this seminar lasted until the 14th. What were the objectives of the Army of Yugoslavia, or rather, the General Staff in terms of future co-operation with the KVM that was expected?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we had already lined up the next group of liaison officers. We thought the current ones would serve for a month or two, and it shows that Yugoslavia was reckoning with long-term co-operation. And the agreement itself said the mission would be working for at least a year. And Yugoslavia was prepared for this work in the long run.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00599.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, thank you for answering my questions. Thank you for appearing as a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my examination is complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a minute to set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Today you've told us about your role as a member of a VJ liaison team with the OSCE and NATO, and we saw a document that my learned colleague showed you which had the composition of this team. This team was headed by General Milorad Obradovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And General Obradovic was assistant chief for operations and staff of the VJ and a member of the VJ General Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you've told us today that you were quite involved in the work of this liaison team, in fact, you told us that you often acted as secretary to this liaison team; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you've also mentioned the fact that the 3rd Army Command, in order for you to fulfil your work as a member of this team, would send this liaison team daily and weekly reports?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And these reports would contain information about the movements of VJ units attached to the 3rd Army in Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, everything that the agreement required us to report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And these reports would also contain information about any incidents involving the VJ which the 3rd Army had -- 3rd Army unit had participated in?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say, sir, that the members of this liaison team were quite well informed of the activities of the units of the 3rd Army in Kosovo during the period that this liaison team existed?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in terms of what we were discussing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you've said the role of this team was to facilitate the work of the KVM, and for this purpose you prepared some instructions that were sent on to the 3rd Army Command and to its units that were deployed in Kosovo, no?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And these instructions included or attached the relevant UN Security Council Resolutions and also copies of the agreements that we've been -- that you've been discussing here today with my learned colleague which you've referred to as the OSCE agreement and the NATO agreement?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: We did that to make sure that our associates are as well informed as possible on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you yourself also had to become quite conversant or well informed of the contents of these different documents, the OSCE agreement, the NATO agreement, and UN Security Council Resolutions?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had the time and we had the space and the documents, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And other members of your liaison team as well had to familiarise themselves with all these documents in order to carry out their work?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I want to start by showing you one of these agreements, which is P837, if we could turn to that. And this is an agreement that you were -- that you discussed with my learned colleague and which you refer to as the NATO agreement is also known as the Clark-Naumann Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I would like to -- if we could go to number 2, Roman numeral II, number 2, both in the English and the B/C/S is the next page. And in the English it's on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you've spoken a bit about this agreement, and this agreement basically contains the obligations that the FRY government accepted to comply with when it was signed; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if we look at number 2, this provision refers to: "Any additional ... heavy weapons ... and equipment brought into Kosovo or transferred to the VJ -- from the VJ to police/special units will be withdrawn from Kosovo or returned to the VJ." This was one of the obligations that was agreed upon pursuant to this agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And a second obligation, if we look at page -- number 4 is that: "All VJ units and additional equipment brought into Kosovo after February 1999 [sic] was to be withdrawn from Kosovo." Correct, sir, that's another obligation that's contained within this agreement?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we see that number 5 provides that: "... all VJ elements remaining in Kosovo will return to garrison except for three company-sized teams which will remain deployed, and the agreement indicates the lines of communication for these three company-sized teams were allowed to be deployed: "The Pec-Lapusnik-Pristina road; Djakovica-Klina; and Prizren-Suva Reka-Pristina ..." So you agree with me, sir, that this agreement only allowed for three company-sized teams to be deployed outside of barracks, and these were the access of deployments that were allowed according to this agreement?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if we look at number 8 - and I believe you've spoken a bit about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we have to scroll down in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This agreement contains, as an obligation to VJ and MUP commanders, to provide KDOM/OSCE, which later became KVM "detailed weekly reports of manning, weapons, and activities of their forces." And also there was an obligation to "provide immediate notification to KVM or Kosovo OSCE of any deployments contrary to these provisions ..." You see, that sir, that that's another obligation that's contained within --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You were asked as well about the mandate or role of OSCE -- we're not going to bring this document up at this stage, but generally you indicated that the main function of the OSCE was to verify the cease-fire between all parties in Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the basic function.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And they were to verify and report on any incidents that occurred in violation of this cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see I've run out of time. I think I will continue on this right after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, right before the break we were looking at the agreement that's before us in the screen, and we had gone over the obligations that the governments of FRY and Serbia had agreed upon when signing this agreement. Now, one of the obligations we saw that had been agreed upon was a reduction of the troop strength to the level pre-February 1998. Now, sir, you would agree with me that in order for the OSCE/KVM mission to verify that this specific obligation of the agreement had been complied with, it required information of the units that had been withdrawn from Kosovo at the time of the signing of the agreement and those that remained in Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in relation to the obligation that concerned heavy weapons, that is, 12.7 millimetres and above, that needed to be also reduced to levels pre-February 1998, the KVM mission would require information about weapons that had been withdrawn with [sic] Kosovo after the signing of this agreement and information on the weapons that remained in the province; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that verification was carried out precisely by KDOM. There was nothing that was in dispute there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you've referred to a meeting between General Ojdanic and General Drewienkiewicz which you yourself attended which took place in -- on 27th November, 1998. You remember speaking about that earlier?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we saw notes of this meeting which were dated 15th December, 1998, which you went over with my learned colleague. You remember that specific document I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, while discussing this document, we saw that one of the points that had been raised by General Drewienkiewicz during this meeting was the need to -- for the VJ to provide information, detailed information, as to the weapons and troop strength on the ground at the time, and we're speaking of November 1998?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that I said in my reply that two or three days after that meeting, I think it was on the 30th of November, we submitted all required information to the mission regarding personnel and arms levels in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We will get to that in a minute. Are you aware, sir, that this meeting was preceded by a request sent by the head of the KVM mission to President Milosevic, where this specific information was requested, detailed information on troop strength and weaponry deployed in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I just heard of the existence of some letter, but I was not aware of the letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Maybe we can look at it together.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It's P838, if that could be brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Here we have the letter. This is dated 23rd November, 1998, and it's -- this was sent a couple days before the meeting you attended, which you spoke about. And if we look at paragraph 3, it indicates: "OSCE requires detailed information on all FRY and Serbian security forces in Kosovo, and the type of information required is specified." This means the armed forces and it indicates which types of units they're referring to, and there's also a chart attached indicating what type of weaponry. So you would agree with me, sir, that this is the type of information that during your meeting with General Drewienkiewicz this is a type of information he was requesting, formation of the units, and also on the weaponry deployed?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, first of all, I'm surprised why this letter was sent to the president rather than to some other bodies, because usually it's not the president who deals with such matters --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: -- I mean, up until then, we hadn't had information --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If I can just stop you there. All I'm asking is if at that meeting that you attended this is the type of information that General Drewienkiewicz asked for. And what we see here is if - and I'm looking specifically at paragraph 3 - this is information, detailed information, on all FRY Serbian security forces, and this means the armed forces, and specific units are indicated there. And also information for those security units at which no formation, unit, or subunit is located, et cetera. So this is the type of information he was asking for specifically, no?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not the way he had put it, but he did mention the letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, and if we look at the next page of the letter, we see there's also - and I'm referring to paragraph 2 - there's also a requirement of information on all FRY security forces, including weapons and equipment, which were withdrawn from Kosovo on 28th October, 1998. And again, my question to you is: This is the information that General Drewienkiewicz was asking for at the meeting that you attended? I'm not asking if he asked for it in the specific same terms as in the letter but if this was the information he was requesting.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot confirm it in that way. Some dates were mentioned, but there weren't any concrete indicators. Only a letter was mentioned. We said that it is KDOM that has this information. As I already said a few days later, we provided information pertaining to units in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm not sure you have answered my question, sir. What I'm asking for is, at this meeting, General Drewienkiewicz asked for specific information on weapons, as is indicated in this letter, no? Including weapons and equipment which were withdrawn from Kosovo by October 28th.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was present, but I hadn't heard of General Drewienkiewicz spelling out his questions in concrete terms. He confirmed all his questions in writing in a letter, but we hadn't had a look at the letter at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But you attended the meeting, no? You spoke about it earlier.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And at this meeting General Drewienkiewicz asked specifically for information on the units deployed and the weaponry that the VJ had in Kosovo at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether that is correct, but I know that we did provide the information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Maybe we can go back and look at the notes from this meeting, and this is 65 ter of the Defence number 76 which you were already shown earlier. And this is D594. I'm sorry, I don't know which tab that is in your binder, but the document will ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. [Interpretation] 12, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that. So if we could go to page 3 in the English, and I believe this is on page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I'm looking for a paragraph that starts with: "General Drewienkiewicz has said that six weeks had already passed" and "time was running out ..." And if we look at the last sentence of that paragraph, have you found the passage, sir? It's on the second page. I believe it's the third paragraph from the bottom up, the last sentence. Have you found the passage, sir?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So we see that General Drewienkiewicz is saying: "... six weeks had already passed, time was running out, and he had no intention of wasting time in drafting a protocol." And the last sentence says: "However, in order to perform the first and any other verifications, it is necessary to send the requested details relating to weapons and strength to the OSCE mission so that it knows what it is to verify -- is to be verified." You see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So what I was asking you earlier and which you indicated you did not have any recollection about is that at this meeting General Drewienkiewicz asked for this same information that we were looking at earlier in the letter, that is, for details on the weapons and troop strength of the VJ; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily. That's not the reply I gave or at least that's not the way I remember it. However, I did say -- or rather, it wasn't clear to me what six weeks General Drewienkiewicz meant, because I know that the mission was rather late. However, this is my specific answer to your question: A few days after the meeting, we submitted information concerning personnel levels and arms levels in Kosovo and Metohija in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. You still haven't answered my question, but I understand that what you're saying is that some days later you submitted information about personnel?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I believe that in an answer to a question of my learned colleague you said that this was done sometime by the 30th of November, if I'm correct, you indicated that day?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I said a few days. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you also indicated when -- in answer to a question by my learned colleague that it was your understanding that the KVM had no mandate to any sort of -- to any sort of arms control, that there was a separate agreement dealing with arms control?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, when it's being done in barracks and also in terms of the agreement on subregional arms control, and the document's based on that. And the OSCE had information about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So the information that you supplied some days after, following this meeting on 27th November, was, in fact, information relevant to the subregional agreement on arms control, if I'm understanding correctly, that's the information that was supplied to the OSCE/KVM?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: However, it so happened that it contained exactly what was required by the OSCE mission, because it pertained to indicators in that period of time and in that area. That is to say, it did not pertain to the entire army. And that's what subregional arms control meant. But it was only the Army of Yugoslavia, just in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you're saying that the information that you provide on the 30th of November in fact indicated the troop levels that had -- that remained in Kosovo after the signing of the agreement and those that had left by 28th of October?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you're also saying that, with relation to the weapons, this information contained the weapons that had been deployed in Kosovo at the time and those that had been withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, I want to show you another document. This is P1001, and this is a letter of 12 December 1998. And I see this document is being brought up. And this is a letter that is addressed to Nikola Sainovic, whom you mentioned earlier was the president of the federal -- or the head of the Federal Commission for Co-operation, and it is sent by the head of the KVM mission, Ambassador Walker. And if we look at the first line it says: "At our meeting on Wednesday," so this is some days prior to the sending of this letter, "we discussed the need for verification base-line information. And we also covered the lack of formal response to my letter ..." And it refers back to the letter we've just looked at and says: "You will recall that the ... information" that's required "is necessary to establish the base-line of forces, weapons, and structures that it," the KVM, "would subsequently have to verify." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So, sir, this letter is being sent almost two weeks after you say information was provided to the KVM, the information that was requested. You would agree with me, sir, that the information that you provided was not the information that General Drewienkiewicz was asking for at the meeting that you had with him and General Ojdanic on the 27th of November?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not familiar with this letter. Now, it can, perhaps, be interpreted that way, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In fact, by this date, sir, the KVM had still not received any information on what is referred to as base-line information, information of the troop strength you had in Kosovo and the weaponry that had remained after the signing of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just repeating that there was an indicator at one of our meetings to the effect that we had sent the required information, the information that was requested from us. Our professional service had compiled this information, we put it all together and sent it. Now, when the Kosovo Verification Mission received them, I don't know, but it couldn't have taken them that long to get there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not challenging the fact that you sent some information to the KVM. What I'm putting to you is that the information you sent was not the information required by the KVM in order to carry out its mandate.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: If that question is being put to me, I cannot confirm it or deny it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But wasn't your role, sir, to liaise with the OSCE and KVM in order to assist the mission to carry out its mandate? Haven't you told us that that was your task, your role as one of the members of this liaison team?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So, sir, you would have been aware, I presume, that by some weeks after you participated in this meeting, KVM was still requesting information on base-line figures. This would have been information available to you as a member of this liaison team of the VJ with the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe it's a question of nuance. Perhaps our reply was not in accordance with Mr. Drewienkiewicz's rubrics, but it was in accordance with our understanding of the matter. Perhaps there was a misunderstanding. This is the first time I see this letter, that we had not completed our task within 15 days. I don't think that that was actually the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So based on that answer, can we agree that although you did provide information, this information may not have been in accordance with what Mr. Drewienkiewicz from the KVM was requesting?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it could be put that way. We believe it was in accordance with the agreement, but perhaps it wasn't in accordance with the rubrics that Mr. Drewienkiewicz had worked out for himself perhaps in a very special way of his own. But may I add that we certainly provided information to Mr. Drewienkiewicz in detail. This information was obtained by KDOM. They had absolute information about units that were leaving barracks in Kosovo and Metohija all the way to this imaginary administrative boundary with Kosovo and Metohija. These are units that had not been stationed originally in Kosovo and Metohija, and they knew what the personnel levels were in both situations. So both NATO and the OSCE did have these indicators at certain points in time, even without our information that we provided later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on from this point, sir. We saw in the agreement that one of the obligations of the VJ was to - and this is number 2 of the agreement which is P837 - that any additional equipment, this is heavy weapons or equipment, brought into Kosovo or transferred to the VJ from the police or Special Police was to be withdrawn from Kosovo, returned to the VJ. Now, sir, do you recall that one of the problems the VJ had in complying with this specific obligation was that the MUP refused to return some of the equipment, heavy weapons, and other equipment that had been transferred by the VJ to Special Police units or to the MUP in general in the summer of 1998? Do you recall that as being one of the problems in complying with this provision?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that I'm not aware of this problem with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay, sir. If we could look -- maybe this reminds you of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could look at P967. The document's still being brought up. And if we could look at page 19 in the English and page 21 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we see there that Lieutenant-General Milorad Obradovic is speaking, and you've told us earlier that he was the head of the team of which you were a member, this liaison team; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So now we see there -- and if we look at the middle of the paragraph it says: "Part of the equipment to the Republic of Serbia a month ago we requested it in writing the return of the equipment so that we could use it in the briefing. MUP informed us today that they would not return that equipment. Actually it includes 20 personnel carriers and 23 mortars that are subject to the OSCE agreement." And these are, I should point out, sir, the minutes of the VJ collegium of 3rd December, 1998. Do you recall that issue being brought up by General Obradovic during the course of your work -- that the MUP was failing to return 20 personnel carriers and 23 mortars?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't doubt that that was the case; however, I cannot present my position in this regard because I did not attend collegium sessions and I don't think that General Obradovic informed us about that. He is speaking here in his capacity of assistant chief, and I'm not aware of these indicators.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I see my learned colleague is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to find the number that my learned friend referred to on this list, but I can't find it on the list and I can't find it in the binder -- and not provided in the notification of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It was notified to the Defence on the 4th of February, I'm being told.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but I can't find it in the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It was notified by e-mail and as an additional exhibit, so -- and I'm seeing nods of heads, so I take it that was received by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, during the course of your testimony today you were shown Exhibit D590, if we could go back to that. Do you recall going through this exhibit earlier with my learned colleague? It's a report from the 3rd Army command mission liaison team, and it's dated 24th December, 1999?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we commented on parts of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your testimony you referred to training, and you indicated the fact that the VJ was allowed to conduct training out of barracks, so that was your understanding of the agreement, prior notification to the KVM?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that -- although the agreement says that it was our duty to provide information as to what had happened in the previous week, that is to say that after things were done, we provided information. At any rate, when the mission was established, we provided information in advance. That is what the direct daily contacts meant. I repeat that the agreement says that we are duty-bound to provide information on movements of units from Kosovo to Kosovo and within the territory of Kosovo for the proceeding week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But we did look at a provision, this was number 8 of the agreement. We went through this together which states the obligation to provide immediate notification to KDOM/OSCE of any deployments contrary to the provisions and explain the circumstances regarding such deployments. Do you recall that, sir, that we went through that together?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've just said that we had these direct daily contacts in which we provided information to the verification mission about these questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this immediate -- this requirement of immediate notification would also apply to situations where the VJ units decided to conduct training exercises outside of barracks; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It is not some training. It is specific training. So, yes; that is correct. I also have to say that very often representatives of the mission followed the column the unit involved when carrying out these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we can look at this report, and it's a report that's sent to the General Staff and to your team, the OSCE and NATO mission liaison team; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we look under the first -- number 1, movement of units of company strength, we see a reference, and it says: "At 0800 hours on 19 December, a reinforced 15th Armoured Brigade tc tank company consisting of" the units indicated there "went to the Batlava airfield sector to carry out planned exercises pursuant to the Unit Combat Training Plan and Programme." Do you see that paragraph where it says that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, this locality is mentioned there, the Batlava airfield sector, that was in the Podujevo municipality, also known as Malo Kosovo area of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that unfortunately I'm not very familiar with the geography of Kosovo, but -- well, this is probably the case. However, I don't seen any problem involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, the Podujevo municipality was a municipality of quite some importance to the VJ because it was bisected by a strategic route that went from Nis to Pristina. Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to sound contradictory, but I have to say that all municipalities in Kosovo are important for the Army of Yugoslavia. Now, as for this specific area, there's a training-ground there where the Army of Yugoslavia carried out training, like any other army. It's an area that was envisaged for such activities. And in this particular case, it is that area called Batlava.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, you're -- you -- I suppose you are familiar, at least in general terms, with the geography of Kosovo and southern Serbia, and you would agree with me that the road going from Nis down to Pristina was an important road, an important supply road?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: An important road generally speaking for the movement of population, for supplies, yes. It's a very important road.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And it was also an important road for supply to the VJ because supplies from Serbia into Kosovo would go down that road, no? The Nis-Pristina road?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Possibly. I did not follow that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Very well. Now, earlier we had looked at the three supply roads that were -- or the three main roads that were envisaged in the agreements along which deployment was authorised. You recall that, that we looked at that earlier?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I think that this involves different reasoning. The troops are in that area only to protect roads, whereas we see that units are in this area for training purposes only. I think that there is a substantial difference involved in terms of what is actually being done and the procedure involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I was just simply asking you, sir, if you remember that when we were looking at the agreements we saw that what was authorised was the deployment of three companies along three axes and we went through that together. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I confirmed that already. I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you would also agree with me, sir, that this road that we've been speaking about, the Pristina-Podujevo-Nis road, was not one of the roads that was envisaged in the agreement along which deployment of troops -- VJ troops was allowed?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: If we are in the context of the text that you refer to, I could not exactly make that kind of comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm asking you a quite simple question, sir. We went over the agreement together. You recall that? We went through the different obligations the VJ had agreed to or the governments of Serbia had agreed to with respect to the VJ and the MUP and the agreement, and we looked specifically at the obligation to -- with -- keep forces in garrison except for three company-sized units that were allowed to be deployed again along certain roads. Do you recall that we looked at that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: We had a look at that, and we agreed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this one was not one of the roads envisaged in the agreement, the Podujevo-Nis road -- Pristina-Podujevo-Nis road?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you, with all due respect, that I do not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us that you were quite familiar with both the NATO and the OSCE agreement as part of your work; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I said that this has to do with training. There is no mention of the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm not asking that, sir. I'm just asking if this specific axis was contemplated in the agreements, and this is something you would know, sir, because it was your job to be fully informed of what obligations the governments of Serbia and the FRY had agreed to pursuant to these agreements, no?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is true that it's not on the list where those units are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I was asking, sir. Before this agreement was signed, the VJ had a company stationed near this training-ground or -- Batlava training-ground; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of these activities. I really know very little about that, except for the few indicators that are contained in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: All I'm asking, sir, I'm not asking about what's indicated in the report. I'm asking whether you're aware that the VJ had a company deployed in this area prior to the conclusions of the agreement we've looked at?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm referring to the report because my activities were related only to the reports of teams that liaised with the missions. I did not follow other reports. Perhaps I knew a little about them, but a very, very little. It was the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps teams that were predominantly involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But you've told us that as part of your work you received weekly and even daily reports from the 3rd Army Command; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say the command. I said the liaison team from the command of the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps. That would be a specific answer. I'm sure that that is what I had said earlier on as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Very well. So you received -- you agree that you received daily and even weekly reports from the liaison teams of the 3rd Army. Now, you've told us that your work was to facilitate the job of KVM and to -- and I presume that also included ensuring compliance with the agreements that we've looked at; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you would have also received information from the 3rd Army liaison teams on how they had carried out their obligations under the agreements, and specifically I'm speaking about the removal of units that were not authorised to be deployed outside of barracks? You would have had that information, no, sir?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot confirm that now, or, rather, I'm claiming that there was no movement of units that were not allowed to move. Units were allowed to be supplied and to train, but I don't see why that would be in contravention of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That was not my question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: However, I see, Your Honours, that we've gone past the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have. We need to break now, and we will resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 11th day of February, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
